result.summary: Pausanias describes Alea, Caphyae and the roads beyond. He records local temples, festivals, the Caphyae reservoir and river Tragus, the old plane-tree of Menelaus, and the story of how Artemis became Apanchomene. He ends with the road to Psophis through the oak-coppice Soron.

scenes.title: Alea and its festivals
scenes.summary: Alea is described, with its founder, temples and the flogging festival of Dionysus.

scenes.title: Caphyae, its waters and plane-tree
scenes.summary: The plain's reservoir, the river Tragus, the town's origins and Menelaus' plane-tree are described.

scenes.title: Artemis the Strangled
scenes.summary: Children bind the statue of Artemis with a rope, are stoned, and the women are afflicted until the oracle orders rites.
scenes.stakes: The children are killed unjustly, and the women suffer stillbirths until the dead are honoured.

scenes.title: Road to Psophis
scenes.summary: The route passes Nasi, the Ladon and the oak-coppice Soron, ending at the boundary of Clitor and Psophis.

alias_notes.explanation: Title meaning 'strangled', given to Artemis at Caphyae after the children's act.

notable_quotes.reason: The children's mock strangling of the goddess's statue starts the aetiological tale.

analysis.text: Cult titles and customs are explained by origin stories, showing how religion marks local memory and guilt.
Pausanias records local oracles, rites and ancient trees, preserving Arcadian traditions of the 2nd century AD.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias compares Arcadian tortoise shells to those of Indian tortoises used for lyres.

language_notes.text: "Argolic league" is an odd phrase; Alea is in Arcadia, so this probably means it was counted with Argive territory or allies.
Spartan boys were flogged at the altar of Artemis Orthia in a ritual endurance test; Pausanias compares it to the women's flogging here.
"Absorbed in the ground" describes a katavothra, a natural sinkhole where water disappears underground and resurfaces elsewhere.
The town's name is said to derive from Cepheus, with "Caphyae" a dialect shortening of the name.
Menelaus, king of Sparta and brother of Agamemnon, gathered the Greek forces against Troy to recover his wife Helen.
The Pythian Priestess was the priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracles.
Apanchomene means "strangled" or "hanged", recalling the children's act in the story.

context_notes.text: Scieria was a festival of Dionysus. Pausanias reports that its flogging of women was ordered by a Delphic oracle.
Ægeus was a legendary king of Athens and father of Theseus, so the Attic origin story is placed in the heroic age.
Pausanias ranks famous ancient trees by age, a common ancient interest; sacred trees were treated as living relics of the past.
Large tortoise shells were used to make the sound-boxes of lyres.

literary_notes.text: The children's game of mock strangling turns into a real tragedy, with trivial play leading to grave punishment.
The stoning of the children sets up the disaster for the women, showing that the crime was a sacrilege and the punishment an injustice.
